the figure reported for 2003.  Of the total value stolen in 2004, 17.3% was recovered, down

100 officers). Crime in Hawaii 2004 also provides data on the time of day, type of  
assignment, and the weapons used in assaults against police officers.

four county police departments, denoting a 3.7% decrease in officers and a 5.5% decrease

•  Trucks and buses accounted for 20.1% (1,484).  Included in this category are pickup

golf carts and other self-propelled vehicles.

**DEPARTMENT OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL PUBLISHES STATEWIDE CRIME DATA AND EXPANDED DASHBOARD**
News Release 2026-54
**FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE**
September 15, 2026
HONOLULU –The Hawaiʻi Department of the Attorney General today published comprehensive statewide crime statistics for 2025 and the next update to the Hawaiʻi Crime Dashboard (https://crimestats.hawaii.gov). The statistics were derived from police data reported under National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS) specifications, through the state’s participation in the FBI’s nationwide Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program. The Department of the Attorney General directs statewide participation in the UCR Program. The online Hawaiʻi Crime Dashboard succeeds the prior “Crime in Hawaiʻi” hard copy publications; several new displays and features were added in the latest update.
Under the nationally standardized definitions and reporting rules of NIBRS, a total of 54,089 “Group A” criminal offenses were reported across Hawaiʻi during calendar year 2025, yielding a rate of 3,775.0 offenses per 100,000 resident population and marking an 11.6% decrease in the state’s total crime rate since 2024. Rate reductions were calculated for crimes against persons (-5.7%) and property (-16.1%), while the rate of crimes against society (e.g., drug and “vice” offenses, weapon law violations) rose 0.9%. A total of 24.5% (13,260) of the reported offenses were cleared by arrest or exceptional means (e.g., death of the offender, offender already in custody in another jurisdiction), marking an increase from the 22.7% clearance rate reported for 2024.

As compared to the tallies in 2024, notable decreases were reported for the following offenses statewide in 2025: murder (-24.2%), negligent manslaughter (-22.2%), forcible sex offenses (-23.4%), robbery (-13.9%), assault (-5.3%), kidnapping (-6.8%), motor vehicle theft (-21.9%), arson (-31.4%), larceny/theft (-19.8%), fraud (-14.7%), counterfeiting/forgery (-19.9%), prostitution (-5.0%) and weapon law violations (-3.5%). Increases were reported for burglary (7.2%), drug offenses (0.2%) and gambling offenses (10.0%). The Hawaiʻi Crime Dashboard presents data for 51 specific offense types.
In the City and County of Honolulu in 2025, a total of 30,758 offenses were reported, yielding a rate of 3,116.3 offenses reported per 100,000 resident population and marking a 16.6% decrease from the total crime rate in 2024. Rate reductions were calculated for crimes against persons (-9.4%), property (-20.7%) and society (-6.9%). The City and County of Honolulu’s total clearance rate increased to 22.4% in 2025, up from 20.6% in 2024.
In Hawaiʻi County in 2025, a total of 10,749 offenses were reported, yielding a rate of 5,110.6 offenses reported per 100,000 resident population and marking a 0.9% decrease from the total crime rate in 2024. Rate increases were calculated for crimes against persons (4.1%) and society (1.8%), while the property crime rate fell 4.2%.Hawaiʻi County’s total clearance rate of 29.5% in 2025 matched the rate reported for 2024.

In Maui County in 2025, a total of 9,284 offenses were reported, yielding a rate of 5,726.8 offenses reported per 100,000 resident population and marking a 6.2% decrease from the total crime rate in 2024. Rate reductions were calculated for crimes against persons (-3.4%) and property (-11.9%), while the rate of crimes against society rose 11.5%. Maui County’s total clearance rate increased to 24.2% in 2025, up from 20.7% in 2024.
In Kaua‘i County in 2025, a total of 3,298 offenses were reported, yielding a rate of 4,494.7 offenses reported per 100,000 resident population and marking a 6.1% decrease from the total crime rate in 2024. Rate reductions were calculated for crimes against persons (-4.5%) and property (-9.8%), while the rate of crimes against society rose 18.9%. Kaua‘i County’s total clearance rate increased to 28.7% in 2025, up slightly from 28.5% in 2024.
Crime victims in Hawaiʻi in 2025 were most commonly male (53.4%), 42.6 years old on average and of Caucasian (47.2%), Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (24.6%) or Asian (23.5%) descent. Arrestees were typically male (71.2%), 42.3 years old on average and of Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (40.5%), Caucasian (33.2%) or Asian (19.7%) descent. The Hawaiʻi Crime Dashboard also allows users to examine the data for several Asian and Pacific Islander racial/ethnic subgroups. (Victims of unknown race/ethnicity were excluded.)

Among the 22,056 victim-offender relationships involved in eligible person and property offenses reported statewide in 2025, the top three relationship types, with unknown relationship types excluded, include stranger (6,160, or 34.2%), acquaintance (2,500, or 13.9%) and boyfriend or girlfriend (2,128, or 11.8%).
Of the 13,639 victims of person offenses eligible for injury reporting statewide in 2025, 5,269 (38.6%) received an injury during the crime incident. The top three most common injury types include an apparent minor injury (4,644, or 34.0%), “other” type of major injury (179, or 1.3%) and severe laceration (162, or 1.2%).
Among the 14,309 offenses that were eligible for weapon reporting statewide in 2025, 13,022 (91.0%) involved the use of at least one weapon type. The top three weapon types in offenses include personal weapons (i.e., hands, fists and feet; 9,785, or 68.4%), “other” weapons (1,217, or 8.5%) and firearms (884, or 6.2%).
The top three most common location types for the 54,089 Group A offenses reported statewide in 2025 include roadways and parking lots (15,408, or 28.5%), residences (14,009, or 25.9%) and commercial establishments (11,475, or 21.2%).
A total of $95,024,747 in property value was reported stolen statewide in 2025, of which 24.4% was recovered, marking a decrease from the 28.2% recovered in 2024. By value subtotal, the top three types of stolen property include money ($31,720,522), automobiles ($20,551,438) and “other” property ($6,371,757).

SSH DATA CHECK: Are car thefts up on Oahu?
Hi folks. This morning, HPD got five stolen-car calls in about an hour, between 8 and 9:10 a.m. with two Downtown, then McCully, Aiea and Waipahu. So we checked what the Honolulu Police Department's own records show for the whole island.
Today is close to a normal day: seven stolen-car calls so far, and October has averaged about eight a day. About four stolen cars a day were found and reported.
Same eight weeks (Aug. 21 to Oct. 16), a year apart:
Vehicle thefts: 416 in 2025, 472 in 2026
Vehicle break-ins: 258 in 2025, 229 in 2026
Month to month, vehicle thefts ran between 194 and 268. March 2026 was the highest month in our records. October has 150 in its first 17 days, and those figures are still filling in.

# Stolen Stuff Hawaii | SSH DATA CHECK: Are car thefts up on Oahu | Facebook
The longer view: the FBI's yearly count for Oahu (the Honolulu Police Department covers the whole island) peaked at 5,255 car thefts in 2021, the most since at least 2010. In 2024 there were 3,878. That is a separate count from HPD's monthly records, so we show it on its own.
The short answer: car thefts are up about 13% on a year ago, but well below the 2021 peak, and break-ins are down. Our monthly HPD records begin in August 2025, so one year is too short to call a trend.

SSH DATA CHECK: Are car thefts up on Oahu?
Hi folks. This morning, HPD got five stolen-car calls in about an hour, between 8 and 9:10 a.m. with two Downtown, then McCully, Aiea and Waipahu. So we checked what the Honolulu Police Department's own records show for the whole island.
Today is close to a normal day: seven stolen-car calls so far, and October has averaged about eight a day. About four stolen cars a day were found and reported.
Same eight weeks (Aug. 21 to Oct. 16), a year apart:
Vehicle thefts: 416 in 2025, 472 in 2026
Vehicle break-ins: 258 in 2025, 229 in 2026
Month to month, vehicle thefts ran between 194 and 268. March 2026 was the highest month in our records. October has 150 in its first 17 days, and those figures are still filling in.

The longer view: the FBI's yearly count for Oahu (the Honolulu Police Department covers the whole island) peaked at 5,255 car thefts in 2021, the most since at least 2010. In 2024 there were 3,878. That is a separate count from HPD's monthly records, so we show it on its own.
The short answer: car thefts are up about 13% on a year ago, but well below the 2021 peak, and break-ins are down. Our monthly HPD records begin in August 2025, so one year is too short to call a trend.

September 15, 2026
HONOLULU –The Hawaiʻi Department of the Attorney General today published comprehensive statewide crime statistics for 2025 and the next update to the Hawaiʻi Crime Dashboard (https://crimestats.hawaii.gov). The statistics were derived from police data reported under National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS) specifications, through the state’s participation in the FBI’s nationwide Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program. The Department of the Attorney General directs statewide participation in the UCR Program. The online Hawaiʻi Crime Dashboard succeeds the prior “Crime in Hawaiʻi” hard copy publications; several new displays and features were added in the latest update.
Under the nationally standardized definitions and reporting rules of NIBRS, a total of 54,089 “Group A” criminal offenses were reported across Hawaiʻi during calendar year 2025, yielding a rate of 3,775.0 offenses per 100,000 resident population and marking an 11.6% decrease in the state’s total crime rate since 2024. Rate reductions were calculated for crimes against persons (-5.7%) and property (-16.1%), while the rate of crimes against society (e.g., drug and “vice” offenses, weapon law violations) rose 0.9%. A total of 24.5% (13,260) of the reported offenses were cleared by arrest or exceptional means (e.g., death of the offender, offender already in custody in another jurisdiction), marking an increase from the 22.7% clearance rate reported for 2024.
texts.1:
As compared to the tallies in 2024, notable decreases were reported for the following offenses statewide in 2025: murder (-24.2%), negligent manslaughter (-22.2%), forcible sex offenses (-23.4%), robbery (-13.9%), assault (-5.3%), kidnapping (-6.8%), motor vehicle theft (-21.9%), arson (-31.4%), larceny/theft (-19.8%), fraud (-14.7%), counterfeiting/forgery (-19.9%), prostitution (-5.0%) and weapon law violations (-3.5%). Increases were reported for burglary (7.2%), drug offenses (0.2%) and gambling offenses (10.0%). The Hawaiʻi Crime Dashboard presents data for 51 specific offense types.
In the City and County of Honolulu in 2025, a total of 30,758 offenses were reported, yielding a rate of 3,116.3 offenses reported per 100,000 resident population and marking a 16.6% decrease from the total crime rate in 2024. Rate reductions were calculated for crimes against persons (-9.4%), property (-20.7%) and society (-6.9%). The City and County of Honolulu’s total clearance rate increased to 22.4% in 2025, up from 20.6% in 2024.
In Hawaiʻi County in 2025, a total of 10,749 offenses were reported, yielding a rate of 5,110.6 offenses reported per 100,000 resident population and marking a 0.9% decrease from the total crime rate in 2024. Rate increases were calculated for crimes against persons (4.1%) and society (1.8%), while the property crime rate fell 4.2%.Hawaiʻi County’s total clearance rate of 29.5% in 2025 matched the rate reported for 2024.

Rate reductions were calculated for crimes against persons (-3.4%) and property (-11.9%), while the rate of crimes against society rose 11.5%. Maui County’s total clearance rate increased to 24.2% in 2025, up from 20.7% in 2024.

Rate reductions were calculated for crimes against persons (-4.5%) and property (-9.8%), while the rate of crimes against society rose 18.9%. Kaua‘i County’s total clearance rate increased to 28.7% in 2025, up slightly from 28.5% in 2024.
Crime victims in Hawaiʻi in 2025 were most commonly male (53.4%), 42.6 years old on average and of Caucasian (47.2%), Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (24.6%) or Asian (23.5%) descent. Arrestees were typically male (71.2%), 42.3 years old on average and of Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (40.5%), Caucasian (33.2%) or Asian (19.7%) descent. The Hawaiʻi Crime Dashboard also allows users to examine the data for several Asian and Pacific Islander racial/ethnic subgroups. (Victims of unknown race/ethnicity were excluded.)

Among the 22,056 victim-offender relationships involved in eligible person and property offenses reported statewide in 2025, the top three relationship types, with unknown relationship types excluded, include stranger (6,160, or 34.2%), acquaintance (2,500, or 13.9%) and boyfriend or girlfriend (2,128, or 11.8%).
Of the 13,639 victims of person offenses eligible for injury reporting statewide in 2025, 5,269 (38.6%) received an injury during the crime incident. The top three most common injury types include an apparent minor injury (4,644, or 34.0%), “other” type of major injury (179, or 1.3%) and severe laceration (162, or 1.2%).
Among the 14,309 offenses that were eligible for weapon reporting statewide in 2025, 13,022 (91.0%) involved the use of at least one weapon type. The top three weapon types in offenses include personal weapons (i.e., hands, fists and feet; 9,785, or 68.4%), “other” weapons (1,217, or 8.5%) and firearms (884, or 6.2%).
The top three most common location types for the 54,089 Group A offenses reported statewide in 2025 include roadways and parking lots (15,408, or 28.5%), residences (14,009, or 25.9%) and commercial establishments (11,475, or 21.2%).
A total of $95,024,747 in property value was reported stolen statewide in 2025, of which 24.4% was recovered, marking a decrease from the 28.2% recovered in 2024. By value subtotal, the top three types of stolen property include money ($31,720,522), automobiles ($20,551,438) and “other” property ($6,371,757).
